articles.author: MaxxMini
articles.description:
Every developer has used a terrible API. Inconsistent naming, cryptic errors, pagination that makes no sense.
After reviewing 50+ production APIs (Stripe, GitHub, Twitch, and plenty of bad ones), I compiled the 7 most common design mistakes — and the exact patterns to fix them.
❌ Bad:
POST /getUsers
POST /createUser
POST /deleteUser

✅ Good:
GET    /users          → List
POST   /users          → Create
GET    /users/123      → Read
PATCH  /users/123      → Update
DELETE /users/123      → Delete

HTTP methods are your verbs. URLs should be nouns. This is REST 101, but 40% of APIs I reviewed still get it wrong.
Exception: Actions that don not map to CRUD use a verb sub-resource:
POST /articles/42/publish
POST /payments/abc/refund

  "firstName": "John",

In Part 1 and Part 2 of this series, we explored Microsoft Agent Framework's core concepts and workflow orchestration. Now we tackle a crucial question: how do your agents interact with the outside world?
Traditionally, each AI framework had its own way of defining tools. Semantic Kernel used KernelFunction, LangChain used @tool decorators, and so on. This created silos—tools built for one framework couldn't be used in another.
Enter the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—an open standard that makes AI tools universal. Build a tool once, use it everywhere.
Model Context Protocol is an open specification (developed by Anthropic and adopted across the industry) that standardizes how AI applications access tools and context. Think of it as HTTP for AI tools—a common language that any…

articles.author: Arjun Krishna
articles.description:
For years, the lakehouse unified storage and analytics.
It did not unify serving.
The architecture typically looked like this:
Lakehouse → analytics & ETL


Operational database → low-latency applications


Reverse ETL → copy curated subsets between them



That split worked when humans drove queries.
AI agents changed the load profile. They issue iterative point lookups, selective filters, repeated joins, and parallel queries inside tight reasoning loops. That workload stresses both scan-optimized engines and traditional OLTP systems in different ways.
Two architectural responses have emerged from Onehouse and Databricks.
LakeBase is positioned as a low-latency serving layer built directly on open lakehouse tables, specifically:
Apache Hudi


Apache Iceberg



Storage remains object-store…
articles.title: Lakehouse Serving: Onehouse LakeBase vs Databricks Lakebase Postgres
